name: autogen

facts.description: A programming framework for agentic AI

title: AutoGen: A Python Framework for Agentic AI and Multi-Agent LLM Applications
answer: AutoGen is Microsoft's open source Python framework for building agentic AI, where multiple LLM-backed agents converse, use tools, and execute code to solve tasks. It sits above model APIs, handling orchestration, inference tuning, and observability. A reader deciding whether to use it should know that version 0.4 introduced breaking changes with a migration guide, so existing 0.2 code and tutorials may need updating before adoption.

sections.body: AutoGen is a programming framework for agentic AI, made by Microsoft and hosted at github.com/microsoft/autogen under a CC-BY-4.0 licence. The repository is written in Python and remains actively maintained, with its last recorded push in April 2026 and roughly 61,250 stars. It appeared publicly as a research-driven project and has since grown into a general framework for building applications in which large language models act as agents. In the AI stack it sits above raw model APIs: it does not train models or serve weights itself, but orchestrates calls to OpenAI-compatible endpoints, Azure OpenAI deployments, and local models, coordinating agents that converse, call tools, and run code. The official documentation site describes it as the official project and states it is not affiliated with any forks or startups.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The framework is used for multi-agent conversation, tool use, code execution, and enhanced LLM inference. Its documentation shows agents configured with an llm_config argument, a config_list of model endpoints, and fallback across models when one fails or is throttled. It supports local inference through OpenAI-compatible servers such as FastChat, demonstrated with ChatGLM2-6B, and enhanced inference features including performance tuning, API unification, caching, error handling, multi-config inference, result filtering, and templating. Research posts show it applied to math problem solving with MathChat and to LLM safety with AutoDefense, a multi-agent jailbreak defense. It is strongest where a task benefits from several specialized agents collaborating, such as analysis, judgment, and coordination roles, rather than a single prompt.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: AutoGen assumes working Python knowledge and comfort with API keys, environment variables, and JSON configuration. The official site offers a migration guide, documentation topics such as LLM configuration and enhanced inference, and blog posts with runnable examples, so a beginner can start from documented patterns rather than source code. Understanding LLM inference parameters helps: the docs explain temperature, top_p, max_tokens, n, and best_of, and warn that temperature and top_p should not be altered together because both control randomness. Some concepts are subtle, including config_list filtering by tags, model fallback order, and the deepcopy behaviour applied to llm_config, which can raise errors for objects that do not support deepcopy. The material does not present a formal prerequisite curriculum, so learners should expect to fill gaps in agent design and evaluation themselves.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem around AutoGen includes OpenAI-compatible clients, Azure OpenAI, local model servers such as FastChat, and the openai-python library, with autogen.oai.Completion and autogen.oai.ChatCompletion available for older openai versions. AgentOps is described as the official agent observability tool, integrated in two lines of code by setting an AGENTOPS_API_KEY and calling agentops.init(), and it tracks LLM calls, costs, latency, agent failures, multi-agent interactions, tool usage, and session statistics. The documentation also points to autogen.code_utils and autogen.math_utils for example evaluation functions. Community evidence is substantial, with tens of thousands of stars, an active repository, and a documentation site carrying blog posts, research write-ups, and migration notes. The site does not quantify contributor counts or release cadence beyond what the repository facts show.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: AutoGen serves both quick experiments and more controlled deployments, though the balance differs by feature. Prototyping is fast because agents are configured declaratively through llm_config and config_list, and local models can be swapped in through OpenAI-compatible endpoints. For production, the framework offers model fallback when an endpoint fails or is throttled, caching, error handling, result filtering, and cost and latency visibility through AgentOps. The documentation notes that n and max_tokens affect token counts and therefore request cost, and that tuning can be done against a validation set with an evaluation function returning metrics. What the material does not provide is benchmark data comparing AutoGen overhead against calling model APIs directly, so the performance cost of the orchestration layer is not settled by the official pages.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The facts show a widely starred Microsoft repository with recent activity, and the site presents AutoGen as the official project, unaffiliated with forks or startups. The documentation frames enterprise readiness around observability, quoting AgentOps on trusting AutoGen in production with monitoring and logging, and noting that observability is a requirement for enterprise-grade agents. Research and blog posts show applied work in math reasoning and jailbreak defense, which indicates academic and safety-oriented use as well. The official material does not name specific companies deploying it, nor does it offer hiring or salary information, so claims about industry adoption beyond the repository's popularity and the AgentOps partnership are not supported. For a developer, it is a current rather than legacy choice, with the caveat that the 0.4 release changed APIs and requires migration from 0.2.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: AutoGen is a Python framework, and its documented integrations assume Python tooling: pip-installed packages, environment variables, JSON config files, and the openai-python client. It is typically used alongside model providers rather than instead of them, whether OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, or local servers such as FastChat exposing OpenAI-compatible APIs. The polyglot pattern it belongs to places AutoGen in the orchestration layer, above inference runtimes and below application code, with observability handled by a separate tool, AgentOps. The official pages read here do not describe bindings for other languages, nor do they compare AutoGen directly with other agent frameworks, so its position relative to alternatives is not established by the material.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The documentation is candid about several limits. Model selection is not automatic: agents generally use the first model in the config_list and fall back on failure, and there is no implicit logic to pick the best model for a task, though some specialized agents may attempt it. The deepcopy applied to llm_config can fail for objects lacking a __deepcopy__ method. Local model setups can require code patches, as shown by the FastChat fix of commenting out finish_reason lines. The 0.4 release and migration guide mean older 0.2 examples may not run unchanged. The site does not state formal support timelines, benchmark comparisons, security guarantees, or governance details, and it does not quantify community size beyond repository stars, so those questions remain open.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
